searchText: cc <@!514429265001971732> thanks! yeah we had some bugs when switching to the standard api - i thought i have fixed everything but still leftovers in the db will go through every block Appreciate the quick analysis from everyone 🙂 Seems like my understanding of fork choice is actually better than I thought after running into this case 😅 <@!755590043632140352> <@!144468805697929216> do you know of a way to get orphan blocks by slot via the current standard-eth2-api? with the prysm-grpc-api you can query all blocks on a slot known by the node there is `/eth/v1/debug/beacon/heads` but only for head You mean after finalization? Before another branch is finalized how can you know if a block is orphaned or not? after finalization yes i mean its nothing i really need, just was wondering Then isn't it easier to traverse the finalization chain backwards until your previous finalized point? it would be cool to query orphan blocks and make them available on the explorer historically Oh I see, I don't thing this is in the standard API but Jim or Radek would know better it is a different thing for the user when she sees "missed block" instead of "orphaned block" Yeah, but you're storing your blocks anyways as you see them, so why not update their status after finalization? right Teku has an option to keep these blocks and a custom api to return them. It’s not currently part of the standard api but I wouldn’t be against adding it. By default I imagine clients would still delete orphaned blocks once the chain finalises past them. That's a little tricky cause this API call would be not so useful before finalization, and certainly cannot be forced on clients to keep them after finalization. I feel like we should strive to keep the standard API to be the really strict minimum we need to require for clients to function in a cohesive way, and this would require some engineering for the benefit of just few It’s still useful before finalisation and it’s up to clients and how they’re configured whether they then keep them. If we keep the standard api to the absolute minimum we’ll wind up with real world use cases like this that have to be implemented using client specific apis. We likely need to move to a place where we can specify standard apis like this but consider them optional, either individually or in a package (eg a set of apis to support light clients). Yeah I wouldn't oppose having a standard that clearly states some points are optional. There's no harn done in suggesting work, there is in demanding it
